subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Google's Secret Car Project
description: A quick, practical guide to Google's Secret Car Project.

hook.text: In 2009, Google quietly hired the top engineers from the DARPA challenges for a secret project.

buildup.text: Sebastian Thrun, who led Stanford's winning team, built a fleet of self-driving Priuses.

discovery.text: Google's cars logged over 100,000 miles on public roads before the public even knew they existed.

twist.text: When Google finally revealed the project in 2010, the cars had already driven more than most teens.

climax.text: The project eventually became Waymo—now the world's most advanced self-driving taxi service.

punchline.text: Google built a car company while nobody was looking.

quiz.question: What did Google's secret self-driving project eventually become?

details.summary: Google launched Project Chauffeur in 2009 as a secret self-driving car initiative led by Sebastian Thrun, which evolved into Waymo and became the most advanced autonomous vehicle program in the world.
details.whyItMatters: Google's early and aggressive investment in autonomous driving gave Waymo a multi-year head start over automakers. It proved that tech companies, not car manufacturers, could lead vehicle autonomy.
takeaways: Project Chauffeur began secretly at Google in 2009
It became Waymo, a standalone Alphabet subsidiary, in 2016
Waymo has logged more autonomous miles than any other company

faq.question: Why did Google, a search company, build self-driving cars?
faq.answer: Google co-founder Larry Page believed autonomous vehicles would save lives and transform transportation. The project also aligned with Google's AI expertise and could generate revenue through mobility services and data.

faq.question: How much has Google invested in Waymo?
faq.answer: Alphabet has invested well over five billion dollars in Waymo. The program has been commercially unprofitable so far, but Waymo's technology lead and growing robotaxi service in Phoenix and San Francisco show progress.
